lessons.title: Leading a dairy team
lessons.html:
The supervisor as team leader

A dairy runs on routines that cannot slip: milking at fixed times, calves fed twice a day, cows fed and moved, plant cleaned. The supervisor turns the manager's plans into daily work done by a team of milkers, calf rearers, feeders and general workers, often starting before dawn and working weekends and public holidays. Your leadership directly affects milk yield, quality and cow welfare.

Leadership versus management

Management is planning, organising and controlling work. Leadership is influencing people to do that work willingly and well. A good supervisor does both: sets clear standards and also earns the team's trust and respect.

Leadership styles

StyleWhen it fits
DirectiveEmergencies, safety issues, new workers learning a routine
CoachingDeveloping workers who are learning and motivated
ParticipativeSolving problems with experienced workers, such as improving the parlour routine
DelegatingSkilled, reliable workers who can run tasks independently

Adapt your style to the person and the situation rather than using one style for everyone.

Building the team

  • Clear roles: everyone knows their tasks, standards and who to report to.
  • Fair rosters, shared transparently, including weekend and holiday cover.
  • Training: new milkers work alongside experienced ones; use written or pictorial procedure cards in the parlour in the languages your team speaks.
  • Recognition: notice and say when work is done well, for example a month of low somatic cell counts.
  • Consistency: apply the same rules to everyone, including friends and relatives.

Leading by example

Arrive on time, follow hygiene and safety rules yourself, handle cows calmly and admit mistakes. Workers copy what supervisors do more than what they say.

lessons.title: Communication, motivation and handling problems
lessons.html:
Communicating well

  • Daily briefings: a few minutes at shift start to cover priorities, problem cows, treated cows and safety.
  • Handover: written and verbal handover between shifts, including cows to be milked separately and any equipment faults.
  • Listening: workers in the parlour and camps often see problems first; ask for their views and act on good ideas.
  • Clear instructions: say what, why, how, by when and to what standard; check understanding by asking the worker to repeat back.

Motivation

People are motivated by fair pay and conditions, but also by respect, recognition, growth and a sense that their work matters. Explain how a clean routine protects the milk price and the farm's future. Offer training and progression, for example from milker to relief supervisor. Address poor working conditions you can influence, such as broken equipment or lack of rain gear.

Managing performance

  1. Set clear, measurable standards: milking start times, teat dipping on every cow, calf feeding records completed.
  2. Observe and give feedback promptly, focusing on behaviour, not the person.
  3. Coach and retrain where the problem is skill.
  4. Use the farm's disciplinary code when the problem is willingness, following a fair procedure and involving the manager.

Conflict

Conflict arises over rosters, workload, favouritism or personal issues. Deal with it early, privately and fairly: hear each side, focus on facts, agree a solution and follow up. Refer serious matters, such as harassment or violence, to the manager immediately.

Safety and wellbeing

Under the OHS Act 85 of 1993, supervisors help ensure that work is done safely. Stop unsafe work, report incidents, make sure protective equipment is used, and watch for fatigue in early-morning and long shifts. Treat people with dignity and comply with labour laws such as the Basic Conditions of Employment Act 75 of 1997.

Key points

  • Combine clear standards with leadership that earns trust.
  • Adapt your style to the person and situation.
  • Use daily briefings and written handovers.
  • Give prompt, specific feedback; coach skill gaps and follow a fair process for discipline.
  • Lead by example on hygiene, safety and calm cow handling.
